author: silver state times
title: University of Nevada program offers hands-on agriculture training for students and apprentices
text:
Some University of Nevada, Reno students are spending their summer gaining practical experience in agriculture through the Desert Farming Initiative’s student summer farm crew, according to a June 17 announcement. Wyatt Diaz, an agricultural science student, said, “I wanted to spend my summer working at the farm because it’s giving me a real hands-on experience in the kind of work I want to do in my career, and I am able to apply my education to the real world. My goal is to one day own and operate a farm.”
The program involves harvesting crops, managing irrigation systems and providing hands-on training in Northern Nevada agriculture. It is part of the College of Agriculture, Biotechnology & Natural Resources’ Experiment Station unit and aims to expand applied training as Nevada’s agricultural industry faces workforce shortages.
Since 2019, more than 25 student interns have participated in academic internships through the Initiative. These internships offer immersive learning experiences in diversified organic production systems alongside staff on hoop house production, field crops, orchard management and plant propagation. Brielle Janas, an environmental science student who will continue with the program as an academic intern into fall semester, said: “I applied for the farm crew position this spring because I am interested in going into agriculture in the future, and working here has already shown me how rewarding the work can be. It has been cool seeing crops go from planting to harvest and knowing I helped with that.”
Beyond internships, the Nevada Farm Apprenticeship Program was launched by the Initiative in 2023. Three apprentices have completed this year-long program so far; graduates now work across Nevada’s food system as farm operators or staff members. Matt Catalano—now hoop house manager at the Initiative—said: “The apprenticeship gave me the foundation to start thinking like a farm operator… I learned not just production skills but how to plan and manage a farm as a business.” Other former apprentices have gone on to lease land or become employed at local farms.
The apprenticeship combines hands-on production training with business development support such as crop planning and marketing strategies; participants also receive mentorship from faculty including Associate Professor Felipe Barrios Masias and Kelli Kelly from the Nevada Small Business Development Center.
Building on its apprenticeship model, an incubator farm pilot is underway supporting three local producers so far; plans call for formal launch later this year. The Initiative also supports broader efforts such as connecting farmers through networks or helping them pursue organic certification. Jill Moe, director of the Initiative, said: “Our goal is to create a clear pathway from student learning and vocational training to agricultural careers and farm ownership… We provide training from seed to market so participants understand how a farm functions as a whole system.”
